questions.question: What is Interdependence (Social Exchange) Theory, and how does it explain relationship maintenance?
questions.solution_html:
• how does it explain relationship maintenance?
  • Answer: Interdependence or Social Exchange Theory (Harold Kelley
  • & John Thibaut) postulates that interpersonal relationships are
  • governed by perceptions of the rewards and costs exchanged in
  • interactions. Rewards include such things as emotional support, status
  • and sexual gratification (in romantic relationships); Costs are such
  • things as the time and energy that a relationship requires.
  • The interactions between acquaintances, friends, and lovers will
  • continue as long as the participants feel that the benefits they derive
  • from the relationship are reasonable in comparison to the costs of being
  • in the relationship. Individuals assess their satisfaction with a
  • relationship by comparing the relationship outcomes (rewards minus
  • costs) to their subjective expectations.
  • Relationship maintenance involves the actions and activities used to
  • sustain the desired quality of a relationship. They can be: Spontaneous
  • (e.g., checking in, shared meals) or Intentional (e.g., visiting
  • family/friends). Both spontaneous and intentional maintenance
  • activities are linked to relationship satisfaction and commitment.
  • Relationship satisfaction is higher when the frequency of maintenance
  • behaviours aligns with expectations or when contributions are
  • perceived as equitable.
  • Why is collaborating considered the most effective conflict
questions.final_answer: Why is collaborating considered the most effective conflict

questions.question: What is Interdependence (Social Exchange) Theory, and how does it explain relationship maintenance?
questions.solution_html:
• how does it explain relationship maintenance?
  • Answer: Interdependence or Social Exchange Theory (Harold Kelley
  • & John Thibaut) postulates that interpersonal relationships are
  • governed by perceptions of the rewards and costs exchanged in
  • interactions. Rewards include such things as emotional support, status
  • and sexual gratification (in romantic relationships); Costs are such
  • things as the time and energy that a relationship requires.
  • The interactions between acquaintances, friends, and lovers will
  • continue as long as the participants feel that the benefits they derive
  • from the relationship are reasonable in comparison to the costs of being
  • in the relationship. Individuals assess their satisfaction with a
  • relationship by comparing the relationship outcomes (rewards minus
  • costs) to their subjective expectations.
  • Relationship maintenance involves the actions and activities used to
  • sustain the desired quality of a relationship. They can be: Spontaneous
  • (e.g., checking in, shared meals) or Intentional (e.g., visiting
  • family/friends). Both spontaneous and intentional maintenance
  • activities are linked to relationship satisfaction and commitment.
  • Relationship satisfaction is higher when the frequency of maintenance
  • behaviours aligns with expectations or when contributions are
  • perceived as equitable.
